newsitem.title: MAURITIUS: Kenya sees two privatised sugar firms by year-end.
newsitem.headline: Kenya sees two privatised sugar firms by year-end.

text.p: Two state-owned Kenyan sugar firms are expected to be privatised before the end of the year, one of which will be listed on the Nairobi Stock Exchange, a government minister said Wednesday.

The two companies earmarked for privatisation this year are Mumias Sugar Co, Kenya's largest sugar firm, and Chemelil Sugar Co, which will be privatised through the sale of government's shares to the public through the Nairobi bourse.

Darius Mbela, Kenya's minister of agriculture, livestock development and marketing said more sugar companies would be privatised later in a bid to raise the East African country's sugar output to a level of self-sufficiency.

"It is widely accepted that the private sector is better suited for efficient production and delivery of commercial goods and services," he told a meeting of the International Sugar Organization in Mauritius.
"To this end, a comprehensive privatisation programme for sugar companies has been drawn up. It is anticipated that by the end of 1997, two companies will be privatised with others to follow later."
Kenya has seven sugar milling factories, five of which are state-owned. Government owns a minority stake in one firm while the other is privately owned.

Mbela said details were being worked on to give priority to small-scale farmers, employees and the public to acquire shares in the privatised firms. Foreign investors were also invited to take shares.

Mbela told Reuters the government would sell a 40 percent stake in Mumias to Britain's Tate & Lyle Plc, local farmers would receive 20 percent of the shares and employees five. The state would retain a sizeable minority stake.
Mbela said the proceeds from the Mumias privatisation would be pumped into the Busia Sugar Co, a new crushing plant which will become operational in 1999.
The Kenyan government had embraced the ideals of economic liberalistion and the sugar industry had not been overlooked, he said.
"Price controls on sugar have been abolished and domestic marketing arrangements of sugar has been liberalised since 1992."
Kenya, a net importer of sugar, produced 389,138 tonnes of the commodity in 1996 -- its best crop in five years. Consumption last year reached 570,000 tonnes.
Sugar prices in the country have been under pressure for some time from illegal imports, Mbela said.
